extracted.intended_audience: central and local government regulators, policymakers, regulatory reform bodies, and stakeholders (businesses, labour, experts) in Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and performance criteria for designing, enforcing, evaluating and reforming regulations in Korea, including tools (RIA, sunset clauses, CICO), enforcement/appeal procedures, sectoral rules (occupational safety), and indices for measuring government and local regulatory performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of unreasonable regulations / consideration of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Abolition of unreasonable regulations by means of public debate or cost-benefit analysis; consideration of other alternatives to the existing regulations if deemed unfeasible; adoption of a priority driven approach to regulatory design, which gives a priority to non-regulatory alternatives, and then to regulatory alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly prioritise non-regulatory options first, then regulatory ones; use public debate and cost-benefit analysis to justify abolition; consider other alternatives if regulation is needed; differentiate regulatory intensity according to level of regulatory conformity; consider non-‘command and control’ enforcement measures such as self-regulation, voluntary agreement, and economic inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and effectiveness of penalty imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of penalty imposition: enhancement of the effectiveness of penalty on regulatory violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties should be designed and calibrated to be effective deterrents; consider proportionality and ways to enhance enforcement impact (e.g. tailoring fines to risk/cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal mechanisms for regulatory enforcement decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-tiered appeal routes: e-petition (Regulatory Reform Sinmungo), civil petitions to the Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission, appeals to the Administrative Appeals Commission, judicial litigation to the Administrative Court, and constitutional complaints to the Constitutional Court after other remedies are exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accessibility (any individual or business regardless of nationality can file), require responsible agencies to amend or explain regulations, provide RRC authority to recommend revisions when refusals are unreasonable; distinguish scope and evidentiary requirements (Administrative Appeals Commission handles narrower/significant infringements with substantive evidence; Constitutional Court reviews constitutionality after other appeals exhausted). Remedies include revocation, nullity affirmation, and orders to perform actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of occupational safety and health regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory objective is to prevent industrial accidents and promote a pleasant working environment to improve workers' safety and health; the Occupational Safety and Health Act provides strategic direction and clarifies responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should aim at maintaining and promoting safety and health by preventing accidents through standards and clarified responsibilities; medium- and long-term plans (five-year plans) are part of policy implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory duties under the Occupational Safety and Health Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Major regulations include requirements for establishing safety and health management systems in workplaces, preventing harm/danger to workers, providing safety and health education, ensuring safety where harmful/dangerous equipment is used, inspecting the working environment, providing medical services (medical check-ups), banning manufacture of harmful materials, prohibiting dangerous work without Ministerial approval, and observing permissible levels of harmful factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties are imposed on business owners; the body of rules comprises an Act, one enforcement degree, and three enforcement rules; industry-specific applicability should be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific scope and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all businesses are required to comply with every provision (e.g., 949 occupational safety articles exist but different industries are subject to different sets of articles); obligations are tailored to industry risks (ensuring safety, risk-prone equipment use, hazard assessment, medical checks for toxic handlers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply regulations proportionately according to industry-specific risks and the relevant subset of legislative provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement in regulatory design
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of representative committees (Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance and Prevention Deliberation Committee; Expert Committee on Occupational Safety and Health) composed of labour, management, government and experts to engage stakeholders in rule-making and legislative amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively involve employers, employees and experts in formulation, review and amendment processes to improve acceptability and effectiveness of regulations; establish specialised committees (e.g., Committee on Industrial Safety Innovation) when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based decisions to strengthen or ease regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions to strengthen or ease regulations are made based on changes in the policy environment and empirical evidence (e.g., industrial accidents concentrated in businesses with less than 50 employees led to a legal obligation for such businesses to appoint safety and health management officers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incidence data and other evidence to justify reinforcement or relaxation of rules; target interventions where problems concentrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of penalties and regulatory relief measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate fines and penalties by factors such as the total cost of demolition and level of potential risk; provide exemptions where overlaps with other laws exist; replace heavy administrative penalties (imprisonment or suspension) with monetary fines where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibrate sanctions to risk and cost; remove duplicative burdens; consider substituting less onerous sanctions to reduce regulatory burden while maintaining safety/effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection, referral and corrective enforcement procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour inspectors monitor compliance, visit high-risk businesses, detect violations, transfer cases to prosecutors for charges, and (after court confirmation) implement corrective measures like monetary fines and penalties or suspension orders for severe infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement follows detection → referral → judicial determination → corrective administrative actions; concentrate inspections on high-risk firms; ensure courts adjudicate alleged infringements before some corrective measures are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of feedback and ex post evaluation mechanisms (Sinmungo & ex post evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulated entities can submit opinions anytime via Regulation Reform Sinmungo; ex post evaluation must be drafted as part of the RIA statement when introducing or reinforcing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use input channels (Sinmungo) for ad hoc evaluation requests; ensure ex post evaluation reviews objective achievement, considers less-regulatory alternatives, and monitors compliance and satisfaction to justify continued existence of regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset clause requirement for retrospective review
rubrics_metrics.description: Central administrative agencies are mandated to include a sunset clause in all regulations unless particular reasons exist not to; sunset clauses take forms of 'review and sunset' or 'outright sunset' with explicit timeframes (usually three years, not exceeding five years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed explicit time-limited review triggers into regulations to induce retrospective evaluation and active revision, improvement, or repeal of ineffective regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-in, Cost-out (CICO) mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: CICO restricts increases in costs of newly introduced or reinforced regulations by abolishing or relaxing regulations that carry an equal or greater amount of costs; responsible agencies must conduct cost-benefit analysis for outgoing regulations that offset costs of new regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require agencies adopting new costly regulations to identify and remove equivalent or greater existing costs; use CICO as a built-in reassessment mechanism for validity, rationality and appropriateness of existing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency regulatory performance assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government Performance Evaluation Committee annually evaluates regulatory reform performance of each central administrative agency; evaluation criteria include the quality of RIA, improvement of existing regulations, and performance of Regulatory Reform Sinmungo; agencies are ranked on a three-tier scale rather than numeric scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update evaluation criteria yearly to align regulatory reform efforts with national agenda initiatives; inform agencies of expected criteria and indicators to ensure whole-of-government coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of institutional tools to monitor and advance regulatory reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and institutional approaches include Regulatory Guillotine, Regulatory Stock Management System, Temporary Regulatory Relief (TRR), expansion of sunset clauses, Ministerial Meetings on Regulatory Reform, and Investment Committee on Emerging Industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt institutional mechanisms and dedicated bodies/initiatives to systematically reduce regulatory stock, provide temporary relief, and promote political support for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futuristic Regulatory Map for emerging industries
rubrics_metrics.description: A top-down forward-looking map to analyse current and future trends of industrial convergence and technological development in selected emerging fields; provides direction for future policy reforms, improvement plans for existing regulations, and rationale for introducing new regulations timed to stages of the industrial cycle (R&D to market development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strategic, stage-based regulatory planning for emerging industries (pilot: self-driving cars) to anticipate gaps and remove obstacles in time for each industry development stage; complement bottom-up business-driven initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local government legal constraints and dispute resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Local governments may enact municipal ordinances and rules within statutory scope but must align with higher legislation; to restrict residents' rights, impose obligations, or penalties they require delegation by Acts; disputes between local governments are mediated by provincial/ministerial heads or Central Dispute Mediation Committee, and unresolved disputes may be brought to the Constitutional Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure local regulations respect hierarchy of laws and required delegations; provide mediation channels for intergovernmental disputes and ultimate judicial resolution via Constitutional Court where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local government regulatory reform duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Framework Act on Administrative Regulations, local governments must register regulations in municipal ordinances/rules, review regulations newly introduced or reinforced, and improve existing regulations in accordance with the central government's regulatory reform framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate local-level regulatory inventorying, review and improvement consistent with national reform objectives to ensure coherence across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business Sentiment Index: assessment criteria and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment criteria include: 1) Appropriateness of regulation; 2) Local governments’ administrative system; 3) Administrative behaviour; 4) Public officials’ attitude; 5) Heads of local governments’ willingness to improve regulation. Assessment elements include licensing, land use and development, operations and marketing activities, constructions and facilities, environment, transparency and deadline compliance, information availability, simplification of paperwork, one-stop services; positive elements (complaints management, active legislative improvement) and negative elements (arbitrary law interpretation, paperwork demands, demands for donations/contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these discrete elements to measure business perceptions of local regulatory administration; combine positive and negative markers to compute a sentiment score for business satisfaction with local regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business Friendliness Index: sectoral assessment elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sector-specific assessment elements covering many policy areas (e.g., building factories and multiple dwellings: land use restriction, floor area ratio, licensing periods; starting restaurant business: ventilation, terrace allowances; supporting start-ups: funding, consulting centres; investment attraction, industrial complex management, distribution/logistics, environmental regulation, public contracting, local tax administration, industrial assistance, public property, urban planning facilities, active administration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess local governments' business-friendliness by measuring concrete administrative and regulatory elements across sectors; use indices to identify regional variation and induce competition among local governments.
